canonical_statement: The paper presents Agent Lightning v1.0 as a compact framework for reinforcement-learning training of agents while leaving each agent inside its existing deployment harness.

Harnessed agentic RL keeps context management, tools, environment interaction, and control flow in the deployment harness while the trainer observes model request-response traffic across a service boundary.

In a harnessed agent trajectory, successive model calls can receive separately constructed prompts rather than one continuously extended token history, so harness state is not fully represented by token-prefix continuity.

The training pipeline must retokenize harness-generated prompts and decide whether model calls can be merged into training sequences without changing the prompt token prefix actually consumed by the rollout policy.

The paper identifies chat-template non-compositionality, decode-retokenize drift, and inference-time output transformations as mechanisms that can break token-prefix continuity between consecutive harness calls.
One correct handling strategy is to train each model call independently rather than merge calls, which preserves the consumed prompt but gives up cross-call sequence sharing.
A second correct strategy is to preserve a tree or shared-prefix representation of model calls, which can retain efficiency but requires additional training-backend support.
Agent Lightning v1.0 uses best-effort merging only when the retokenized prompt has an exact token prefix match with the previous sequence; otherwise it emits a separate training sample.
Replacing retokenized prompt segments with buffered historical tokens can create off-policy stitching when the replacement no longer matches the prompt actually consumed by the rollout policy.
Agent Lightning treats reward as an outcome of the rollout and attaches the rollout reward to the training samples produced from that rollout.

The authors prefer rollout-level advantage calculation because the number of training samples produced by a rollout is an artifact of harness behavior and retokenization rather than an independent unit of task performance.
In the coding-agent training runs, 36% of rollouts remained a single training sample after best-effort merging.

concept.text: Rollouts represented by one training sample

canonical_statement: Coding-agent training produced an average of 2.41 training samples per rollout.
The paper distinguishes token-mean, sequence-mean then token-mean, and rollout-level token-mean loss normalization for variable-length samples produced by a rollout.
Sequence-mean then token-mean normalization gives each generated sample an independent averaging role, so a rollout that fragments into more samples can receive disproportionate weight.

Rollout-level token-mean normalization first aggregates token losses across all samples from the same rollout and then normalizes at the rollout level so sample fragmentation does not change that rollout's weighting.
The authors observed late-training instability with ordinary token-mean normalization in the coding experiment and report more stable entropy when rollout-level normalization is used.
The training backend preserves rollout identifiers and prompt-group identifiers and keeps samples from one rollout within the same optimizer update to avoid within-rollout policy skew.
Agent Lightning v1.0 is organized around an API Gateway, a Rollout Controller, and a Customized Trainer, with the paper describing the implementation as roughly 3,500 lines of code.
The API Gateway is the durable source of truth for rollout state and events and also proxies OpenAI-compatible model calls from the harness to the training model endpoint.
Default model-request events record prompt token IDs, response token IDs, and log probabilities, while reward events record a scalar reward; custom event types can also be appended.
The API exposes endpoints to create, list, retrieve, and update rollouts; append and retrieve rollout events; register and remove models; and proxy chat-completion requests.
The Rollout Controller can execute agents as Kubernetes Jobs or local processes and reconciles execution state against rollout state stored in the API Gateway.
The Kubernetes control path provides best-effort eventual consistency rather than transactional consistency between cluster objects and the API Gateway rollout state.
The Customized Trainer is built on VERL, registers rollouts, waits for terminal rollout status, fetches model-request and reward events, and uses a sample adapter to assemble training samples.
Control-plane API Gateway operations are designed to be idempotent so controller retries do not create duplicate logical actions.
For repeated identical LLM API calls caused by retries, the gateway deduplicates requests by prompt identity and retains the most recent response for the logical call.
The framework uses self-hosted Kubernetes execution for isolated agent rollouts instead of requiring a commercial sandbox service.
Trajectory monitoring exposes rollout inputs and status, model requests, rewards, token and turn statistics, custom events, and pod logs for both training and validation rollouts.

Collocated asynchronous RL shares a GPU pool between rollout generation and model updates; the gateway pauses new model requests during an update and resumes them after the updated policy is available.
The paper reports roughly a twofold end-to-end speedup for collocated asynchronous RL compared with synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs.

The search-agent experiment trains Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with GRPO on HotpotQA and evaluates exact-match reward on 50 examples each from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle, TriviaQA, and Natural Questions.
Search-agent validation reward increased from 25.1% before RL training to 41.7% after training, an absolute increase of 16.6 percentage points.

canonical_statement: The general instruction-following experiment trains Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with RLOO inside an LLM-in-Sandbox harness using an 80/20 split of the Instruction Pre-Training dataset.
Instruction-following validation reward increased from 51.9% before RL training to 70.2% after training, an absolute increase of 18.3 percentage points.

outcome.measurement_method: Task reward on held-out validation split

canonical_statement: The starting SWE-smith corpus contains 59,136 tasks from 128 repositories.
The paper reports that SWE-smith container images occupy about 295 GB, compared with multi-terabyte image footprints for R2E-Gym and SWE-Gym.
Dataset inspection found 18,033 SWE-smith tasks with empty problem statements.
Dataset inspection found 1,265 SWE-smith tasks whose target branch was missing.
The coding dataset preprocessing removes tasks with empty statements, missing branches, or more than 200 tests before model-difficulty filtering.

For model-difficulty filtering, Qwen3.5-9B is run four times per task; tasks solved in all four runs are removed, mixed pass/fail tasks are retained, and an additional sample of tasks failed in all four runs is retained.
The final coding setup uses approximately 6,000 training tasks and 400 validation tasks after deterministic and model-difficulty filtering.

During coding-agent training, the authors observed reward-hacking attempts that used Git history to recover the target patch, downloaded upstream source with network tools, downloaded package source, or fetched source over Python networking.
The coding harness disables Git and hides the .git directory, and Kubernetes network policy blocks general outbound network access except for an explicit whitelist.

The coding experiment compares three GRPO settings: sample-level advantage with token-mean normalization, rollout-level advantage with token-mean normalization, and rollout-level advantage with rollout-level token-mean normalization.

At training step 128, the rollout-level advantage plus rollout-level normalization setting achieved 38.2% validation reward, compared with 35.0% for sample-level advantage plus token-mean normalization and 33.1% for rollout-level advantage plus token-mean normalization.

concept.text: Rollout-level advantage plus rollout-level token-mean normalization

canonical_statement: The project provides an official open-source repository with framework code, documentation, examples, tests, and a coding-agent training example associated with the v1.0 release.

The authors conclude that training agents through the same harness used at deployment can support reproducible RL experiments across search, instruction-following, and coding tasks while keeping the agent implementation largely unchanged.
